Source: docs/manual/concepts/animation.md
Canonical: https://rainerweston.github.io/goblin-node-docs/manual/concepts/animation/

---
id: concepts.animation
title: Animation and Time
description: Understand frame ranges, playback time, looping, and animation export.
kind: concept
audience: intermediate
app_since: 1.6.0
platforms: [ios]
last_verified: 2026-09-08
owners: [editor, texture-engine, export]
related_features: [animation, node-time, animation-export]
writing_mode: reference
---

# Animation and Time

Animation settings store frames per second, an inclusive start frame, an inclusive end frame, and the seamless-loop choice.

The default range is frame `0` through frame `59` at 30 frames per second. The current preview frame is session state and does not make the graph dirty.

The **Time** node can provide seconds, the current frame, or normalized progress. A one-frame range produces normalized progress of `0`.

Animation export supports at most 1000 rendered frames and requires Pro. Seamless Loop reserves an extra unrendered endpoint so the last authored frame remains below normalized progress `1`.


---

Source: docs/manual/concepts/bit-depth.md
Canonical: https://rainerweston.github.io/goblin-node-docs/manual/concepts/bit-depth/

---
id: concepts.bit-depth
title: Bit depth
description: Choose between ordinary, high-precision, and floating-point graph processing.
kind: concept
audience: intermediate
app_since: 1.6.0
platforms: [ios]
last_verified: 2026-09-08
owners: [texture-engine, export]
related_features: [bit-depth, export-formats]
writing_mode: reference
---

# Bit depth

Bit depth controls how precisely a graph stores image samples. More precision can reduce banding and preserve a wider numeric range.

Eight-bit processing stores ordinary bounded samples. Native 16-bit processing preserves more steps for supported nodes. The 16F mode can preserve finite negative and above-one values through supported paths.

Unsupported nodes can downgrade a branch to eight-bit processing. The preview is a bounded display projection and is not proof that an export preserves the same numeric range.

PNG and TIFF support unsigned 16-bit grayscale export. OpenEXR preserves 16F values in the current floating-point export path.

---
id: concepts.graph-flow
title: How graph flow works
description: Understand how nodes, ports, and connections produce a texture.
kind: concept
audience: beginner
app_since: 1.6.0
platforms: [ios]
last_verified: 2026-09-08
owners: [editor, texture-engine]
related_features: [graph-connections, graph-rendering]
writing_mode: reference
---

# How graph flow works

A graph is a procedural recipe made from connected nodes. Each node creates data or changes data from an earlier node.

An output port sends data. An input port receives data. A connection carries the data from the output port to the input port.

Flow matters because Goblin Node evaluates upstream sources before downstream results. A **Checker** node can feed **Box Blur**, which can then feed **Graph Output**.

```text
Checker -> Box Blur -> Graph Output
```

**Graph Output** identifies a result that the Output preview and export tools can use. A branch that does not reach an output can still appear in the Selected preview.

Learn how to [connect nodes](../workflows/connect-nodes/) or [make your first texture](../start-here/first-texture/).

---
id: concepts.persistence
title: Local persistence
description: Understand where Goblin Node stores graphs and assets on iOS.
kind: concept
audience: intermediate
app_since: 1.6.0
platforms: [ios]
last_verified: 2026-09-08
owners: [project-browser, persistence]
related_features: [local-first-storage, graph-history]
writing_mode: reference
---

# Local persistence

Goblin Node uses local IndexedDB storage on iOS for graphs, assets, and catalog data.

Graph history is local to the device. It does not currently have a restore interface.

Graph packages provide the portable transfer path. Dormant cloud-sync code does not make current graphs available across devices.

Source: docs/manual/concepts/ports-and-channels.md
Canonical: https://rainerweston.github.io/goblin-node-docs/manual/concepts/ports-and-channels/

---
id: concepts.ports-and-channels
title: Ports and image channels
description: Understand typed connections and grayscale, RGB, and RGBA image data.
kind: concept
audience: beginner
app_since: 1.6.0
platforms: [ios]
last_verified: 2026-09-08
owners: [node-registry, texture-engine]
related_features: [ports, image-formats]
writing_mode: reference
---

# Ports and image channels

An input port receives data, and an output port sends data. Compatible ports form a connection.

Image data can contain one grayscale channel, red-green-blue channels, or red-green-blue-alpha channels. Alpha stores transparency.

Channel nodes separate or combine image channels. Value nodes send typed parameter data, such as a float, integer, Boolean value, enumeration, or two-component vector.

Goblin Node can promote data to a wider channel layout when a node contract supports it. Some nodes intentionally return grayscale or opaque color.


---

Source: docs/manual/concepts/resolution-inheritance.md
Canonical: https://rainerweston.github.io/goblin-node-docs/manual/concepts/resolution-inheritance/

---
id: concepts.resolution-inheritance
title: Resolution inheritance
description: Understand how a node selects its output width and height.
kind: concept
audience: intermediate
app_since: 1.6.0
platforms: [ios]
last_verified: 2026-09-08
owners: [texture-engine]
related_features: [render-resolution, resolution-inheritance]
writing_mode: reference
---

# Resolution inheritance

Resolution inheritance lets a node get its output size from the graph or a connected input.

**Relative to Parent** starts from the graph resolution. **Relative to Input** starts from the node's authoritative input. A scale then changes that base size.

Some nodes define a special dimension source. Image Sample uses **Coordinates** when connected, then **Image**, then the graph dimensions.

Pixel-based modes use explicit output pixels. Their relative footprint changes when the graph resolution changes.

# Basic animated texture

![Animated texture preview](../examples/basic-animated-texture.svg)

This example connects **Time** to **Graph Output**. It uses frames `0` through `59` at 30 frames per second.

1. Download the [graph package](/goblin-node-docs/manual/examples/basic-animated-texture.gnproj).
2. Import the package from the Project Browser.
3. Open the imported graph.
4. Start preview playback.
5. Watch the output change across the frame range.

The normalized Time value progresses from the first frame toward the final frame.

NOTE: Graph package import and animation export require Pro.

# Manual downloads

Download the [current Goblin Node User Manual PDF](/goblin-node-docs/manual/manual-current.pdf) for offline reading or printing.

Meaningful app releases preserve an immutable, versioned PDF in the [release archive](https://github.com/rainerweston/goblin-node-docs/tree/main/manual/releases/manuals). The live website can receive documentation corrections between app releases.

The PDF identifies its app version, documentation revision, generation date, and canonical website. Generated PDFs must not be edited manually.

---
id: start.first-texture
title: Make your first texture
description: Build and adjust a procedural checker texture in about five minutes.
kind: tutorial
audience: beginner
app_since: 1.6.0
platforms: [ios]
last_verified: 2026-09-08
owners: [editor, documentation]
related_features: [graph-editing, node-library, output-preview]

---

# Make your first texture

Build a checker texture and view it in the Output preview. You will add nodes, make a connection, and change a parameter.

## Before you start

Open Goblin Node and create a graph. Keep the node library and Output preview visible.

## Build the graph

1. Find **Checker** under **Generators > Pattern**.
2. Drag **Checker** into the graph.
3. Find **Graph Output** under **Graph**.
4. Drag **Graph Output** to the right of **Checker**.
5. Drag from the **out** output port on **Checker**.
6. Release the connection on the input port of **Graph Output**.

The checker pattern now appears in the Output preview.

## Change the pattern

1. Select **Checker**.
2. Set **Squares** to `16`.

The preview now shows more, smaller squares. Goblin Node recalculates downstream nodes after a parameter changes.

## Try one change

Set **Squares** to `4`. Compare the larger squares with the previous result.

## Common mistakes

- If the preview is blank, check that the connection ends at **Graph Output**.
- If the wrong controls appear, select **Checker** again.
- If a panel is closed, use its toolbar control to reopen it.

## Next steps

- [Connect nodes](../workflows/connect-nodes/)
- [How graph flow works](../concepts/graph-flow/)
- [Checker reference](../nodes/checker/)
- [The preview is blank](../troubleshooting/blank-preview/)


---

Source: docs/manual/troubleshooting/blank-preview.md

---
id: troubleshooting.blank-preview
title: The preview is blank
description: Restore a blank Selected preview or Output preview.
kind: troubleshooting
audience: beginner
app_since: 1.6.0
platforms: [ios]
last_verified: 2026-09-08
owners: [editor, texture-engine]
related_features: [selected-preview, output-preview, graph-connections]
writing_mode: strict
---

# The preview is blank

The Selected preview or Output preview shows no texture.

## Most likely cause

The preview has no valid source. A missing connection or the wrong preview target commonly causes this symptom.

## Fix the Output preview

1. Find **Graph Output** in the graph.
2. Check its input for a connection.
3. Connect an image-producing node to the input.
4. Select that output in the Output preview.

The connected texture should appear.

## Fix the Selected preview

1. Select an image-producing node.
2. Open the Selected preview.

If the preview stays blank, reload the graph and repeat the check. Preserve the graph package before reporting a repeatable rendering failure.

See [Connect nodes](../workflows/connect-nodes/) for the connection procedure.

---
id: editor.connect-nodes
title: Connect nodes
description: Send an output from one node into an input on another node.
kind: workflow

---

# Connect nodes

Create a connection so one node can send data to another node.

## Procedure

1. Find the source node.
2. Drag from its output port.
3. Move the pointer to a compatible input port.
4. Release the pointer.

The graph shows a connection between the two ports. The downstream result updates in the preview.

## If the connection does not appear

1. Check that you started from an output port.
2. Check that the destination is an input port.
3. Try another compatible input port.

See [How graph flow works](../concepts/graph-flow/) for the direction and purpose of data flow.

# Export textures

Export a configured Graph Output result from the editor.

1. Open the Output preview.
2. Select the required graph output.
3. Display the export dialog.
4. Set the file format.
5. Set the naming options.
6. Confirm the operation.

A single encoded file uses the iOS save or share flow.

Multiple output files create a ZIP archive. Batch export and animation export require Pro.

# Import assets

Add an asset that an Image node or palette workflow can use.

1. Open **Assets** in the Project Browser.
2. Open the asset picker.
3. Choose a supported source.
4. Review the new asset in the catalog.

iOS can offer file, camera, or photo-library choices when the operating system permits access.

Palette imports accept palette assets that use PNG, HEX, or Adobe ASE data.

Source: docs/manual/workflows/import-export-graphs.md
Canonical: https://rainerweston.github.io/goblin-node-docs/manual/workflows/import-export-graphs/

---
id: workflows.import-export-graphs
title: Import or export a graph package
description: Move graphs or a custom node library between Goblin Node installations.
kind: workflow
audience: intermediate
app_since: 1.6.0
platforms: [ios]
last_verified: 2026-09-15
owners: [project-browser]
related_features: [graph-transfer, node-library, collections]
writing_mode: strict
---

# Import or export a graph package

Use a `.gnproj` file for a graph without bundled assets. Use `.gnpack` when the export includes assets or dependencies.

Use a `.gnpackage` file to share a collection as a custom node library. Collection package transfer requires Pro.

## Export

1. Select a graph in the Project Browser.
2. Open the graph transfer action.
3. Choose the required package options.
4. Export the package.

## Import

1. Open the Project Browser.
2. Open the package importer.
3. Choose a `.gnproj` or `.gnpack` file.
4. Review the package details.
5. Confirm the import.

Graph package import and export require Pro. Package import creates a graph rather than replacing an open graph.

## Export a custom node library

1. Mark a collection as a node library.
2. Open the collection action menu.
3. Select **Export .gnpackage**.
4. Select optional unreferenced assets from the collection.
5. Export the package.

The package always includes nested collections, graph dependencies, and referenced assets.

## Import a custom node library

1. Open the Project Browser.
2. Select **Import .gnpackage**.
3. Choose a `.gnpackage` file.
4. Review the collection, graph, and asset counts.
5. If items are invalid, select the option to import valid items only.
6. Confirm the import.

Import creates a new top-level collection and does not replace an existing library. The library is visible on the importing device by default.

# Manage graphs in the Project Browser

Use the Project Browser to manage graphs, assets, collections, and Trash.

## Create and organize a graph

1. Open the Project Browser.
2. Create a graph.
3. Enter a distinct name.
4. Move the graph into a collection when you need catalog grouping.

## Recover a graph

Items moved to Trash remain available for restoration. Open **Trash**, select the graph, and use the restore action.

CAUTION: A purge permanently removes the selected item. Confirm the target before you purge it.

# Preview graph results

Choose the preview that matches the result you need to inspect.

1. Use the Selected preview to inspect the selected node.
2. Use the Output preview to inspect a configured Graph Output result.
3. Use the 3D preview to inspect assigned material maps on a mesh.

The size and bit-depth badge describes the current two-dimensional preview result. Preview controls do not change exported pixels unless they change graph or export settings.

Source: docs/manual/workflows/save-graphs.md

---
id: workflows.save-graphs
title: Save a graph
description: Preserve graph changes and recover from a failed save.
kind: workflow
audience: beginner
app_since: 1.6.0
platforms: [ios]
last_verified: 2026-09-08
owners: [editor, persistence]
related_features: [project-save, autosave, local-first-storage]
writing_mode: strict
---

# Save a graph

Save after a meaningful graph change or before leaving the editor.

1. Press the save control.
2. Wait for the saving state to finish.
3. Confirm that no save-failed notice appears.

Autosave can preserve later changes. A failed save keeps the graph dirty and permits another manual or automatic attempt.

If saving fails, keep the editor open and retry after the connection or storage problem clears.

        "inputNotes": [

          "Tiling may cause visible seams when used with strong spherical distortion."
        ],
        "behaviorNotes": [
          "Spherize remaps UVs using a spherical projection function centered at the given point.",
          "Intensity controls the radius of the spherical effect with negative values inverting the direction."
        ],
        "inputNotes": [
          "Requires an image input to distort."
        ],
        "outputNotes": [
          "Outputs the spherized image with the same dimensions."
        ],
